A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, framework, benchmark and image-steering method. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original human studies of ten image generators, five LLMs and alternative image-steering mechanisms, with numerical results in Sections 3–4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds steerability prediction, cross-model decomposition estimates, classifier-free guidance experiments and a professional prompt-engineer study.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4 adds a trained CLIP-based steerability predictor combining prompt/image embeddings, model identity and a regression head, then uses predictions to estimate cross-model decomposition components. The original benchmark and Thompson-sampling image-steering procedure remain; the latter is now described as using learned proposals.

E1.justification: Coverage expands to five professional prompt engineers completing 34 steering rounds and to steerability prediction using existing survey data. PixelProse images, geometric tiles and headline rewriting remain covered; moving the headline study to Appendix B.2 does not remove that task.

E2.justification: The new prediction experiment compares the full model/image/prompt predictor against data-mean, model-only and model-plus-prompt predictors (v2 Figure 4). The original image-generator and LLM memberships, and the text/random-image/RL-image steering comparison, are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds an 80/20 train/test prediction protocol evaluated with R² and MSE, plus CLIPScore-based alignment evaluation. New surveys allow CFG values from 1–10, recommending 4, on SD3.5 Medium and evaluate experts on SD3.5 Large Turbo. The original five-attempt benchmarks and 60,000-episode RL training remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether poor steering reflects limited guidance controls, novice users or prompt-image misalignment (Appendices B.4–B.5 and Figure 6). Predictor feature ablations and cross-model decomposition further investigate variation in steerability (Figure 4). Existing blind-rewrite, seed-choice and constrained-seed analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Section 4 introduces Monte Carlo estimation of the new decomposition using predicted conditional rewards, a statistical estimation procedure absent from v1. Standard-error reporting otherwise remains consistent; additional result rows do not establish increased repetitions or a changed uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: New results include predictor R²=0.493 and MSE=0.508, alignment correlation 0.32, CFG mean scores of 0.670 without versus 0.679 with guidance control, and final scores of 0.670 for regular users versus 0.741 for experts. Original image-steering scores are unchanged between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 1. Figure 2 exchanges DALL-E 3 and SD3.5-large-turbo labels while retaining bar heights, conflicting with the retained ranking in v2 Figure 5.

T1.justification: v2 Equations 4–5 introduce a cross-model decomposition using output distributions and conditional expected rewards to separate mechanism and producible-distribution contributions. Appendix A supplies its derivation. This extends v1's reward-gap framework; the earlier benchmark and RL mathematics are largely retained.

C1.justification: v2's introduction adds predicting steerability and explaining cross-model differences as central contributions. Its poor-steerability claim explicitly extends to professional prompt engineers. The original benchmark contribution and greater-than-twofold image-steering improvement claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets estimated cross-model improvements as roughly half mechanism-related and half producibility-related, while explicitly stating that the decomposition is not causal. It also distinguishes user intent from prompt-image alignment and adds discussion of longer-term learning, copyright and steerability-related misuse. These extend v1's interpretation beyond its artificial seed tradeoff.

D1.justification: v2 adds A100 hardware information for prediction, clarifies that edited prompts are submitted from scratch, and reports analysis-script and README availability in the checklist. It omits some earlier details, including the three-rater majority rule for improvement ratings and the reported five-second image-generation latency.

R1.justification: v2 adds references connecting its analysis to economic decompositions, classifier-free guidance, shared-CLIP failures and Artwhisperer. It removes several references, including Church et al., Chang et al.'s evaluation survey and Shu et al.'s RewriteLM. Most related-work discussion and the positioning around isolating steerability remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative is substantially compressed and reorganized: the LLM study moves from Section 3.2 to Appendix B.2, detailed RL exposition moves to Appendix C.2, and cross-model comparison becomes a central section. Metric descriptions are condensed, steering terminology changes, and the conclusion and checklist expand.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. v1 Table 1 and Figure 3 are combined into v2 Figure 3; new prediction/decomposition and alignment displays and CFG/expert tables are added. Existing plots move into the appendix, and the headline example table is transposed and condensed.

improvement.justification: The added CFG, expertise and alignment checks directly test alternative explanations for v1's findings, while the formal decomposition makes cross-model comparison more explicit. These strengthen the paper, although the five-expert sample and prediction-dependent, noncausal attribution limit the gain. Figure 2 also introduces a ranking inconsistency with Figure 5. The substantive checks provide a modest net benefit despite that reporting defect.
